overview: Sigma's AutoTool switches to the fastest digging tool while the attack key is held. The EventTick handler returns immediately unless keyBindAttack is pressed and the mouse-over carries a block position, then delegates to BlockUtils.updateTool, which scans the nine hotbar slots for the item with the greatest getStrVsBlock against the targeted block and writes inventory.currentItem directly. The module never constructs packets: the C09 held-slot change is emitted by the fork's PlayerControllerMP.syncCurrentPlayItem whenever the tracked slot diverges at the next interaction, and the C07 dig pairs are the vanilla clickBlock stream.

sections.p: updateTool iterates the hotbar with a strength accumulator that starts at 1.0F and a strictly greater-than comparison, so a bare hand (1.0 strength) never wins and the first slot that beats the current best is kept; ties favor the lowest index. The selection is purely getStrVsBlock against the targeted block state: there is no durability weighting, no enchantment-aware ranking and no silk-touch or fortune logic, so the module picks the raw fastest dig and will happily choose a nearly broken tool over a fresh one.

The write goes through the public currentItem field, and the C09 comes from PlayerControllerMP.syncCurrentPlayItem, which is called at the top of the interaction entry points (clickBlock, onPlayerDamageBlock, onPlayerRightClick and the rest) and emits C09PacketHeldItemChange only when the tracked slot diverges from the field. Because the switch happens while the attack key is held, the C09 lands immediately before the vanilla C07 START and STOP dig pair of the next break, producing the C09(tool), C07 pair, C09(restore) fingerprint around each dig when the player switches back.

The module is inert while the attack key is released, and it bails when objectMouseOver is null or carries no block position, so it only fires at an actually targeted block. It never touches the inventory window, never ranks armor or offhand state, and has no settings at all: the constructor is empty, which makes the module a pure convenience layer over the vanilla dig path.

files.label: AutoTool.java
files.explanation:
The module file is a thin gate: it returns unless keyBindAttack is pressed, objectMouseOver is non-null and carries a block position, then calls BlockUtils.updateTool(pos) once per tick. There are no settings and no packet construction; the entire mechanism lives in the util it delegates to. The EventTick registration places the handler on the per-tick event fired from EntityPlayer.onUpdate, so the switch is re-evaluated every tick the attack key is held.

The empty constructor and the absence of state make the module's surface easy to bound: it only writes inventory.currentItem, and everything observable on the wire comes from the vanilla interaction path reacting to that write.

files.label: BlockUtils.java (updateTool)
files.explanation:
updateTool (lines 65-82) is the selection engine: it reads the targeted block state, walks hotbar slots 0-8 with a strength accumulator starting at 1.0F, keeps the first item whose getStrVsBlock strictly exceeds the current best, and writes inventory.currentItem. The strict greater-than comparison against a 1.0F floor means an empty hand never wins and the first best slot wins ties, a lowest-index bias that is worth knowing because it is what the module actually does, not a weighted ranking.

The same file shows the family's other helpers the module does not use: updateDirections sends a C05 look packet when collided vertically, and the liquid and ground probes are unrelated to tool selection. For AutoTool the file's relevance is exactly updateTool and its write-through to currentItem, which is the hook that makes the fork's syncCurrentPlayItem emit the C09.

countering.label: FastBreak (tool-calibrated break duration)
countering.explanation:
FastBreak is NCP's dig-duration check and it is invisible to this module by construction. The expected breaking time comes from BlockProperties.getBreakingDuration, which reads the item in the main hand and walks the full tool table (type, efficiency level, haste and aqua affinity effects, on-ground and in-water penalties), so the check already assumes the player is using the optimal tool for the block. AutoTool's switch makes the client behave exactly like that assumption: the dig completes in the per-tool expected time, elapsed plus the 10ms delay is never below expected, and the fastBreakPenalties bucket never accumulates.

The honest boundary runs the other way: a true fastbreak hack that shortens the dig below the tool-calibrated expectation trips FastBreak immediately, which is why the check is the family's anchor. Against a best-tool switcher it scores nothing, because the module's entire effect is bringing the client's behavior up to the level the check already models as legitimate.

countering.label: Frequency (blocks per time frame)
countering.explanation:
Frequency counts break events against time windows rather than dig durations: 2x1000ms ActionFrequency buckets with an interval weight of 45 in survival by default, plus a short-term counter that allows 7 break events inside 5 ticks before flagging. It counts completed breaks, not slot changes, so the module's only contribution to the ledger is the dig cadence itself, which is vanilla: the tool switch adds no break events of its own.

The check would catch a module that multiplied dig rate, but AutoTool leaves the C07 stream at the player's natural click pace. The slot-switch traffic between digs is invisible to Frequency, which is exactly why the family pairing of FastBreak (duration) and Frequency (rate) still leaves the C09 fingerprint to the slot-side checks and the honest gap entry.

countering.label: Reach (blockbreak distance)
countering.explanation:
Reach is NCP's blockbreak distance check: it measures the eye-to-block-center distance against 5.2 blocks in survival (5.6 creative) and accumulates excess into the violation value. AutoTool's tool switch grants no reach whatsoever; the player digs from the same position with the same ray that the vanilla path already validated, so the measured distance is identical to a manual dig.

The check matters to the family because some dig helpers move the player or extend the interaction range to reach distant blocks; this module does neither. Reach therefore contributes an honest pass, and its presence in the set documents that the module's surface is the slot switch, not geometry.

countering.label: UseItemAdapter (held-slot handler)
countering.explanation:
UseItemAdapter's onChangeSlot handles PlayerItemHeldEvent: on a real slot change it calls requestItemUseResync, which forcibly releases an item in use so a held-slot switch cannot mask an ongoing eat or block. For AutoTool the handler is inert: the switches happen between digs, outside any item use, so there is no in-use state to release, and the resync path never fires.

The entry is the documented gap of the family: no NCP check scores the C09-to-C07 pairing that is AutoTool's actual fingerprint. The slot change is only observable at the protocol level (the C09 before the dig), and NCP's only held-slot hook is the item-use resync, which by design ignores switches that occur while nothing is in use. Servers that want the pairing need a protocol-level switch-and-dig check, which this tree does not ship.
